title: Quantum polynomial-factor approximation of Euclidean SVP
formal:
Do there exist a real constant \(C>0\), an integer \(k\geq1\), a real constant \(K>0\), and one uniform quantum algorithm \(A\) with the following property? For every pair of integers \(d\geq n\geq1\) and every explicitly given matrix \(B\in\mathbb Q^{d\times n}\) with linearly independent columns, the algorithm terminates within \(K(N+1)^k\) charged operations on every execution and outputs a nonzero integer vector \(z\in\mathbb Z^n\), with
\[\Pr\!\left[\|Bz\|_2\leq n^C\lambda_1(L(B))\right]\geq\frac23.\]
Here \(N\) is the full binary input length, \(L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\}\), and \(\lambda_1(L(B))\) is the length of its shortest nonzero vector. The probability is over the computation’s measurement outcomes on this fixed classical input. All constants and the program are chosen before the input; the approximation exponent depends on neither rank nor coefficient size.
definitions:
The input contains \(d,n\) and all \(dn\) rational entries in row-major order. To fix a binary encoding, let \(b(t)\) be the ordinary binary expansion of a nonnegative integer \(t\), using the one-bit string \(0\) for zero, and put \(E(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t)\). Dimensions use \(E(d),E(n)\). A rational number is encoded by a sign bit followed by \(E(|a|)E(q)\), where it equals \(a/q\), \(q>0\), and \(\gcd(|a|,q)=1\); zero has positive sign and denominator one. There are exactly \(dn\) entries and no trailing bits. Valid inputs satisfy \(d\geq n\geq1\) and column independence over \(\mathbb Q\). The total number of encoded bits is \(N\). The polynomial clock applies on every binary input; behavior and output on malformed or dependent-basis inputs are otherwise unrestricted.

The Euclidean norm of \(v\in\mathbb R^d\) is \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^d v_i^2)^{1/2}\). The lattice consists of all integer combinations of the columns, with its usual embedding in \(\mathbb R^d\). Independence makes \(z\mapsto Bz\) injective and makes \(L(B)\) discrete in its real span. Thus
\[\lambda_1(L(B))=\min_{z\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}}\|Bz\|_2>0\]
is attained. No uniqueness of the shortest vector up to sign is assumed. The algorithm returns the coefficient vector: its \(n\) signed integer coordinates use a sign bit and \(E\) of the absolute value, with positive sign for zero. It must return a valid nonzero vector on every execution on a valid input. An unsuccessful execution may exceed the norm bound, but may not output zero, fail to halt or omit the vector. The squared norm can equivalently be used in the displayed guarantee with squared factor \(n^{2C}\).

A uniform quantum algorithm means one finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine controller with classical input, work and output tapes and a collection of initially zero qubits. In addition to ordinary bit-machine steps, it may apply a gate from \(\{H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\}\) to explicitly addressed qubits, or measure an addressed qubit in the computational basis and receive its classical result. Qubit indices are written in binary on control tapes; writing and processing them take ordinary charged steps. Initializing a fresh zero qubit is charged, so the number of qubits is also polynomially bounded. The input is supplied as classical bits, not as a quantum state-preparation oracle. Classical input bits may be transferred to qubits through charged computation.

For computational basis states \(|0\rangle,|1\rangle\), the gates are
\[H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4}),\qquad
\mathrm{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin\oplus b\rangle,\]
where \(a,b\in\{0,1\}\) and \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. A register of \(q\) qubits has state a unit vector in \((\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes q}\). A gate acts on its addressed factors and as the identity elsewhere. Measurement outcome \(a\) has probability equal to the squared norm of the projection onto the subspace whose measured bit is \(a\), after which the state is that normalized projection. Classical control may depend on all earlier outcomes. Probabilities of complete executions are defined by these conditional Born probabilities. Fair classical random bits can be generated by a Hadamard gate followed by measurement; their cost is included.

Each classical Turing-machine step, gate, initialization, measurement and output-bit write costs one operation; any fixed overlap in bookkeeping changes only the constant \(K\). The stated bound holds on every possible measurement branch, including unsuccessful branches. There is no quantum advice, computational oracle, free input oracle, postselection on rare outcomes or arbitrary-precision unit-cost arithmetic. The program is independent of input length and of the particular basis. All classical control, including input parsing and generation of the quantum operations, contributes to the same bound.

The approximation parameter is the rank \(n\), not the ambient dimension \(d\) or the bit length \(N\). In rank one the factor is exactly one. Coefficients may have arbitrary binary length, subject only to being part of the input. There is no promised gap between successive vector lengths, random input distribution, special ring structure, modular form or bound on the basis conditioning. Success is required separately on every valid basis, not on average over bases.
answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence of one algorithm and fixed constants \(C,K,k\) satisfying the entire statement, or of its logical negation. A negative answer must rule out every constant polynomial approximation factor and every uniform quantum algorithm with any fixed polynomial clock in the full bit length; an impossibility for one exponent, one circuit family, one oracle model or classical algorithms alone is insufficient. A valid positive answer must prove the actual nonzero-vector output and success probability on all valid inputs, with every-execution cost including classical processing. A decision algorithm for a length threshold, an algorithm assuming a unique shortest direction, a conditional cryptanalytic reduction, or a numerical experiment is not by itself an answer. Conditional results establish only their conditional conclusions unless the additional assumptions are proved. This is an exact existence proposition; the benchmark’s numerical tolerance does not weaken its approximation or probability requirements.
why: This isolates whether quantum computation changes the polynomial-time approximation boundary for unrestricted Euclidean lattice search. A positive answer would improve the guarantee from a superpolynomial loss to one fixed power of rank on every lattice. A negative answer would establish an unconditional limitation on general quantum computation, far beyond the failure of any particular quantum lattice algorithm. Its cryptographic implications depend on the exact lattice task and approximation exponent.

importance.reason: A foundational quantum-algorithm question with broad relevance to lattice complexity and computational cryptography. The model and accuracy combination is distinct from both existing classical approximation and quantum exact-search cards.

progress.text: LLL supplies a classical polynomial-time algorithm with an exponential-in-rank approximation guarantee; this historical bound is recorded in Bennett’s survey.

Brakerski–Kirshanova–Stehlé–Wen relate LWE and extrapolated dihedral cosets with explicit parameter losses; the checked full revision is dated May 23, 2019.
Regev posts the 2009 article with a correction to the proof of Claim 3.13; this is not a new polynomial-time lattice algorithm.
Chen’s author correction withdraws the stated polynomial-modulus LWE algorithm claim because of a Step 9 bug.
Zhang’s version 8 retains explicit extra access and front-end assumptions in its post-processing result.

The Gupte–Ragavan–Zhandry response is revised; it states an algorithm-specific refutation and provides Lean code whose proof execution was not independently checked in this audit.

context_blocks.text: Long basis vectors need not imply a large lattice minimum. The two columns \((M,1)\) and \((M+1,1)\), with integer \(M\geq1\), generate a lattice containing \((1,0)\), although both input columns are long. The objective concerns all nonzero integer combinations. It differs from finding the shortest input column and from minimizing over real coefficients, where arbitrarily small nonzero combinations exist.

Bennett’s survey defines approximate search SVP by the same multiplicative comparison with \(\lambda_1\). It records the classical polynomial-time LLL guarantee \(2^{O(n)}\). The factor \(n^C\) requested here is a much stronger bound for every fixed \(C\), while allowing any such constant is a substantial relaxation of exact shortest-vector search. Small-dimensional experiments or guarantees for a particular basis family do not cover this quantifier order.

The decision problem \(\gamma\)-GapSVP is given a basis and a threshold \(r>0\), with a promise of either \(\lambda_1\leq r\) or \(\lambda_1>\gamma r\), and asks which case holds. It does not output a vector. Bennett’s §4.2 explicitly records the unresolved general search-to-decision connection with polynomially controlled approximation. This card does not silently identify those two tasks. Likewise, unique-SVP assumes that every vector linearly independent of a shortest vector is longer by a promised factor; unrestricted SVP has no such promise.

Regev’s original worst-case-to-average-case theorem says that an efficient solver for specified Learning With Errors parameters yields quantum algorithms for the stated GapSVP and shortest-independent-vectors tasks. Learning With Errors supplies random linear equations with a controlled noise distribution; it is not the classical arbitrary-basis input specified here. The direction, task and parameter losses of a reduction matter. In particular, this theorem is not an unrestricted equivalence between polynomial-factor search SVP and every LWE family.

The Brakerski–Kirshanova–Stehlé–Wen paper explicitly describes Regev’s dihedral-coset reduction as a reduction for unique-SVP, then establishes an LWE connection with extrapolated dihedral cosets under parameter losses. Such coset problems supply particular quantum samples as input. Their efficient solution is a separate claim whose consequences for an arbitrary classical basis require a proved reduction with the appropriate target.

The April 2024 Chen manuscript initially claimed new polynomial-time quantum lattice and LWE algorithms. Its archive entry includes an explicit April 18 author correction: a bug in Step 9 invalidates the stated polynomial-modulus LWE claim, with no repair then known. The surviving old abstract is therefore not evidence of a verified breakthrough.

Zhang’s May 14, 2026 revision analyzes a conditional replacement for part of that procedure. Its current statement requires additional front-end conditions and access to a run-dependent offset residue; the introduction explicitly says the resulting LWE conclusion is conditional. These assumptions do not form a complete arbitrary-basis algorithm in the model of this card. Earlier stronger-looking descriptions are not substituted for the latest revision.

Simon’s ePrint 2026/1591, first posted August 3 and last revised August 17, explicitly advertises a polynomial-time dihedral-coset algorithm and polynomial-factor SVP consequences. The archive also records a correction to the first draft’s Lemma 3 and the author’s acknowledgment of a subsequent refutation. The available abstract alone does not verify the asserted unrestricted search consequence or its bit-complexity conventions. The claim is recorded as disputed, not as a resolution.

Gupte, Ragavan and Zhandry’s response, revised September 1, states that Simon’s August 11 algorithm cannot recover even the secret’s least-significant bit with nonnegligible advantage. They provide accompanying Lean 4 code. The repository describes precise rounding and register conventions, and a theorem about the specified bit-output procedure and controllers of its coarse outcomes; it explicitly distinguishes this from a formalization of the full-secret recursion. This audit read those scope declarations but did not build or independently verify the proofs, and could not retrieve either ePrint PDF. The rebuttal is evidence against that proposed algorithm, not a lower bound against all algorithms on this card.

The accompanying repository explicitly states that its full-secret solver recursion is not formalized and that its controller theorem observes prescribed restart/bit outcomes rather than every internal measurement record. Those declared limits must be retained when describing what has been machine checked by its authors.

A classical solution of TCS-6667 with the matching factor would also solve this quantum existence target, and an exact quantum solution of TCS-7169 would supply the stronger approximation guarantee. Neither implication reverses automatically. An algorithm here would be a major lattice-complexity advance, but declaring a particular cryptosystem broken would require checking its problem variant, parameters and reductions.

sentences: A lattice consists of all integer combinations of a linearly independent rational basis, and its shortest nonzero vector can be much shorter than every basis column.
The question asks whether one uniform quantum algorithm finds a nonzero vector within a fixed power of the rank of that optimum on every explicitly given basis.
Its probability of meeting the length bound must be at least two thirds per input, with polynomial total bit cost on every execution and classical vector output.
Known reductions for decision or uniqueness-promised lattice problems do not by themselves establish this unrestricted search guarantee.
An August 2026 claimed lattice consequence and its September algorithm-specific rebuttal are recorded as disputed evidence with explicit verification limits.
